messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 42
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Factory Worker
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 73

**Vignette: Amara, Age 42**

Amara came to this country seven years ago carrying almost nothing — a small bag, a borrowed phone number, and a silence she has never quite been able to explain to anyone. Before she left her home country, she had been a schoolteacher, a mother of two, a woman known in her neighborhood for her loud laugh. That version of herself feels like someone she read about once, a long time ago.

She was detained for eleven days by government forces following a protest she had attended with her brother. What happened during those eleven days — the beatings, the electric shocks applied to her hands and feet, the hours spent hooded in a stress position, the sounds of others being hurt nearby — she does not speak about in sequence. She speaks about it in fragments, when she cannot stop herself, and then she goes very quiet for the rest of the session. She says she was released only because a relative paid a bribe. She does not know what happened to two of the men who were detained with her.

She has worked for four years at a poultry processing plant on the edge of the city. The work is cold and loud and relentless, and she is grateful for it in the way that people are grateful for things that keep them too exhausted to think. She stands at her station for eight-hour shifts, moving through the same motions, and she tells herself this is manageable. Most days it is. But the smell of the plant — something metallic and organic at once — sometimes sends her somewhere else entirely. She finds herself back in that room, hands bound, heart hammering, certain she is about to die. She has learned to grip the conveyor belt rail when this happens and count backward from one hundred until the floor feels solid again. Her coworkers think she is simply quiet. She prefers it that way.

Sleep is the part of her life she dreads most. She delays it as long as she can, staying up past midnight watching videos on her phone with the brightness turned all the way down, because lying in the dark feels like being hooded again. When she does sleep, she is often back in detention — not always in the same scene, but always with the same certainty of helplessness, the same knowledge that no one is coming. She wakes with her heart slamming, sometimes shouting, and then sits on the edge of her bed for an hour, ashamed of the noise she has made in an apartment with thin walls.

Her marriage ended three years ago. Her ex-husband, also a refugee, told her she had become unreachable — that she flinched when he touched her unexpectedly, that she could not sit with her back to a door, that she left rooms without explanation and did not come back. He was not wrong. She knows she pushed him away and she knows she could not have done otherwise. Her children, now teenagers, live with her and navigate around her moods with a carefulness that breaks her heart. She sees them watching her and wonders what they understand.

She describes herself as someone who used to be curious about people and now finds them mostly exhausting and faintly threatening. She does not go to community gatherings. She does not attend her children's school events unless she can stand near an exit. She has stopped calling her sister back home because the calls make her feel the distance too acutely, and also because her sister sometimes asks questions she cannot answer.

What brings her to therapy, she says, is not the nightmares or the hypervigilance or the smell of the plant. It is that her younger son recently told her he is afraid of her — not of what she might do, but of the way she sometimes looks at him as though she does not know where she is. She says she will not let him grow up afraid of his own mother. That, she says, is the one thing she will not allow.
